claim: Reflected XSS occurs when a user-controllable value is placed inside a CSS `background-image` `url()` context with a `javascript:` URI, because the browser resolves the URI and executes the script during page rendering regardless of HTML encoding applied elsewhere.
mechanism: The CSS parser in WebKit and Blink resolves `url()` values and follows protocol-relative URIs; when the reflected value contains `javascript:` followed by executable code, the browser's style engine passes the URI to the network layer which interprets it as a script request, and if the page lacks a restrictive Content-Security-Policy or X-Content-Type-Options headers, the fetched script executes in the page's origin. This mechanism holds even when the value is HTML-entity-encoded elsewhere, because the CSS `url()` context performs its own decoding after the HTML parser has already placed the raw text into the style attribute.
disproof: The claim is false if the browser's CSS `url()` implementation completely strips the `javascript:` protocol and refuses to fetch it, or if the server consistently applies a Content-Security-Policy `script-src 'self'` directive that blocks the fetched script from executing, or if the reflection is stripped of all `javascript:` sequences at the HTTP level before reaching the CSS context.
novelty: NEW

claim: A JSON API endpoint reported as XSS is valid even when the response has `Content-Type: application/json`, because the reflected value can reach an HTML-executing context through client-side framework binding that assigns the JSON response body into `innerHTML` or a template that re-interprets the text as HTML.
mechanism: The fetch request returns JSON with a structure that a JavaScript framework assigns via `.innerHTML = data` or interpolates via template literals `${data}` in HTML-binding contexts; the framework deserializes the JSON string and renders it as markup, and if the reflected value contains angle-bracket-delimited script, the browser parses and executes it. This mechanism works even though the initial response header claims `application/json`, because the cross-context flow from API consumer to HTML sink creates the XSS at the sink, not at the API endpoint.

novelty: the item_key xss.fp_rule.json_api.content_type_json_is_not_html_execution already covers the general principle; my claim specifies the additional mechanism of client-side framework binding as the cross-context conduit.

claim: The WHATWG HTML parsing algorithm fixes which insertion contexts turn reflected bytes into executable script, so exploitability is a property of the parser state the reflection enters, not of the payload string alone.
mechanism: The HTML tokenizer runs through distinct states — data, tag open, attribute value (quoted/unquoted), script data, RAWTEXT/RCDATA, comment — and the same byte sequence means different things in each: '<' opens a tag in data state but is inert inside a quoted attribute value, and '</script' closes a script element only in script data state. Cheat sheets (OWASP XSS Prevention, CWE-79) therefore require per-context output encoding (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL), because an encoder valid for one state does not neutralize the same characters in another.
disproof: False if a payload executes identically in every context the application uses with no parser-state dependence — e.g. the actual sink is a client-side eval() or innerHTML assignment that ignores the server-side HTML context entirely, making insertion-context analysis inapplicable.
novelty: NEW — adjacent to xss.fp_rule.html_encoding.entity_encoded_reflection_cannot_break_context (which asserts the encoding FP rule), but no corpus item states the parser-state mechanism as the normative determinant of exploitability.

claim: A reflected payload blocked by a deployed Content-Security-Policy remains an XSS finding under CWE-79 and OWASP guidance, because CSP is classified as defense-in-depth rather than a primary XSS control.
mechanism: CWE-79 classifies by root cause — improper neutralization of input during web page generation — which exists at the sink whether or not a compensating control currently blocks execution. OWASP's cheat sheets prescribe output encoding as the primary fix and describe CSP as an additional layer that can be bypassed (allowlisted hosts, JSONP endpoints, script gadgets, report-only deployment, policy relaxation on deploy), so an app relying on CSP alone has not met the normative requirement.
disproof: False if the policy is enforced (not report-only), blocks every vector available to the payload (no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval, no allowlisted domain serving attacker-controllable script, no sink gadgets on the origin), and cannot be weakened server-side — then no execution path exists and the candidate is a non-finding.
novelty: NEW — xss.test.execution.confirm_in_real_browser mentions CSP report-only only as an execution-confirmation caveat; no corpus item decides whether a CSP-blocked reflection is still a finding.

claim: The normative XSS rule applies at the sink, so a client-side sink such as innerHTML, document.write or eval receiving attacker-influenced data is a finding even when the server response is clean JSON that never renders the value server-side.
mechanism: In DOM-based XSS the malicious value can travel entirely within the browser — from a source like location, location.hash or a message event — into a sink whose semantics (per WHATWG/MDN) re-parse or execute strings: innerHTML parses as an HTML fragment, document.write into the document stream, eval compiles as script. OWASP's DOM XSS guidance therefore treats source-to-sink taint flow, not server response content, as the object of the test, so a JSON API response feeding innerHTML is exploited at the browser sink.
disproof: False if the client code path is provably absent — the value is bound only through textContent or a framework's auto-escaping template with no raw-HTML escape hatch and never assigned to any sink — in which case no execution path exists and the candidate is a false positive.
novelty: NEW — xss.fp_rule.json_api.content_type_json_is_not_html_execution's disproof names the innerHTML path, but that item is an FP rule about Content-Type; no corpus item asserts the sink-level normative rule for DOM XSS.

claim: A payload whose only source is a client-side channel (URL fragment, window.name, postMessage, referrer) is genuine XSS even though no byte of it ever appears in any HTTP request or response the server logs.
mechanism: The server serves an unmodified static or pre-rendered document; the victim's browser then reads an attacker-controlled value from a location that is never transmitted — the fragment after '#' is stripped before the request is sent — and hands it to a sink such as innerHTML, document.write, or an eval'd string. The reflection test looking for a marker in server responses therefore never fires, yet the script executes in the origin, so absence of reflection in the wire traffic is not evidence of absence of XSS.
disproof: Every end-to-end execution path is traced and shown to originate from a value that arrived in an HTTP response or request body server-side, with no fragment/name/postMessage source contributing to the sink input.
novelty: NEW — no item_key in the corpus addresses DOM-only sources; xss.test.entrypoints.unique_alnum_marker_sweep only covers server-reflected entry points.

claim: A payload split across a boundary that a WAF and the origin parse differently (chunked transfer boundaries, double-encoded or overlong UTF-8 sequences) will be reported as "blocked" while the origin assembles and executes it, so a WAF block is not proof of non-exploitability.
mechanism: The WAF inspects its own normalized byte stream, while the origin server performs a second, independent decode — dechunking, percent-decoding, charset transcoding — after the WAF has already made its verdict. If the two disagree by even one byte (the WAF sees `%253c` as an encoded percent, the origin sees `<` after a second decode; or the payload straddles two chunks so neither chunk alone matches a signature), the request that reaches the application is the fully assembled script, so the request that reaches the application is the fully assembled script while the WAF's log records a clean or blocked request.
disproof: A payload constructed to differ between the two parsers (e.g. split at a chunk boundary or double-encoded) is consistently rejected by the WAF *and* the origin never receives the assembled bytes — demonstrated by the origin's own access log showing no execution.
novelty: NEW — the corpus has no WAF/proxy-normalization item; xss.fp_rule.json_api.content_type_json_is_not_html_execution concerns response content type, not request-side parser divergence.

claim: A strict CSP (nonce or hash-based script-src, no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval) does not downgrade a confirmed XSS to non-exploitable when the injected markup is consumed by an already-allowed script or an injected javascript: navigation target.
mechanism: The CSP header only constrains which script *sources* may be parsed and run; it does not constrain what data existing trusted scripts write into the document. An injected value that reaches a sink inside whitelisted application code (an allowed script that reads the reflection and assigns it to innerHTML, or an attribute like href that a trusted handler later navigates) executes with the page's full authority, and event-handler attributes or javascript: URLs are only blocked where the policy actually omits 'unsafe-inline' *and* the sink is not a trusted script's data flow — so the wire-level header gives a false sense that the injection is inert.
disproof: Under that exact CSP, an end-to-end attempt with the injected markup fails to execute through any allowed path — no trusted-script data flow to an HTML sink exists and the report-only/enforced header is verified present on the executing response — with execution confirmed by a second observable as the corpus requires.
novelty: NEW — no item_key covers CSP interaction with exploitability; xss.test.execution.confirm_in_real_browser governs how to confirm execution, not whether a policy has already neutralized it.
